Southwest Research Institute® U.S. DOE Award Number DE-FE0032301 Public Version - 18 - DE-FE0032301 Final Report SECTION 4 — Challenges, Intellectual Property, and Resolutions 4.1 Technical Challenges and Resolutions During system development and testing, several technical challenges were identified that influenced both electrical and mechanical performance. Each issue was systematically evaluated and resolved to ensure safe, reliable, and repeatable operation during the later high-flow and engine-integration phases. Early bench-scale testing revealed electrical arcing within the gas- delivery section of the reformer caused by insufficient insulation surrounding the high-voltage electrode. The arcing produced localized damage to one power-supply channel and interrupted testing. The issue was mitigated by adding dielectric insulation, revising electrode spacing, and repairing the damaged electrical circuit. Subsequent testing confirmed stable operation with no recurrence of discharge faults. The power-electronics subsystem experienced thermal overload during high-frequency operation as transistor junction temperatures exceeded design limits. This was corrected by paralleling switching transistors to distribute current load, adding additional heat-sinks, and refining temperature interlock thresholds. The upgraded configuration maintained component temperatures within safe margins during extended high-duty operation, improving reliability for continuous testing. The rapid current changes in the plasma pulses generated electromagnetic noise, which radiated into nearby cables and circuits, temporarily disrupting data collection and causing device shutdowns. Shielded cabling, improved grounding, and optimized cable routing eliminated the problem. These design adjustments ensured that plasma operation did not interfere with instrumentation or engine controls during later integration testing. Another benefit is that the reformer can be positioned upstream in the fuel line to minimize electrical noise impact on critical engine components. A minor but instructive challenge occurred during high-flow operation at the SwRI MRF, where localized melting of an insulator was observed near the high-voltage connector. As illustrated in Figure 15, the damage resulted from capacitive charge buildup within redundant Kapton insulation layers that allowed discharge along the polymer surface. The design was modified by removing the excess insulation and reconfiguring the connector geometry to minimize field concentration. No further thermal degradation was observed after the correction, and the issue provided useful insight for future high-voltage design optimization. Following these corrective actions, the plasma reformer demonstrated consistent ignition behavior, stable power delivery, and reliable operation across a range of laboratory, facility, and engine tests. No additional electrical or thermal faults were encountered during the final months of testing. 4.2 Intellectual Property Development The project resulted in a patent disclosure covering a novel pulsed-power approach for plasma generation.
